The incubation period for Pavonine cuckoo (Dromococcyx pavoninus) eggs, when maintained under controlled laboratory conditions closely mimicking natural nest temperatures of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], has been documented to span approximately 11 days [ab = approximately 11 days]. This relatively brief incubation phase is characteristic of many brood-parasitic cuckoos, likely reflecting selective pressures to synchronize hatching with the host nest's developmental schedule. Upon emergence, the altricial nestling exhibits a remarkably low wet weight at birth, measuring just 2.6 grams [Wwb = 2.6 grams]. This neonatal mass is substantially smaller than the values reported for non-parasitic members of the Cuculidae, a disparity that may be linked to the reduced parental investment inherent in brood parasitism. The newly hatched chick is entirely dependent on the host parents for provisioning and thermoregulation during its first days of life. At the typical body temperature of this species, near 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], field surveys tracking individual nests have shown that the period between hatching and achieving sustained flight is approximately 23 days after birth [tx = approximately 23 days after birth], allowing the juvenile to vacate the host nest before competition for food becomes critically intense.

Following fledging, the young bird enters a protracted juvenile stage characterized by continued growth and plumage maturation. Under the standard thermal regime of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C] that typifies the species' resting state, the onset of puberty, indicated by the first detectable signs of gonadal recrudescence, occurs around 69 days after birth [tp = around 69 days after birth]. This timeline aligns closely with the attainment of near-asymptotic body dimensions. Measurements from a geographically representative sample of museum specimens indicate that the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult Pavonine cuckoo reaches approximately 46.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 46.4 grams]. This modest adult body mass places D. pavoninus among the smaller members of the Neotropical cuckoo guild, a factor that likely influences its host selection strategy. Comparative analyses with congeneric species suggest that the total duration of the juvenile phase, from independence to the threshold of reproductive competence, represents a significant portion of the overall lifespan, a pattern typical of tropical altricial birds that require extensive foraging experience to succeed as brood parasites.

The species' reproductive strategy is heavily constrained by its obligate brood-parasitic lifestyle, with females depositing exactly one egg per host nest [N_R_i = one egg per host nest]. This single-egg-per-nest tactic minimizes the risk of detection by the host and ensures that the cuckoo nestling faces minimal competition from conspecifics within the same brood. At the typical body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the maximum rate at which a single female can achieve successful parasitism has been estimated at approximately nine eggs per year [Ri = approximately nine eggs per year], a figure derived from long-term field studies tracking marked individuals across multiple breeding seasons. This moderate annual fecundity is typical of specialist brood parasites that must carefully time each laying event to coincide with the host's own egg-laying window. The age at which a female first attempts her own brood is a critical demographic parameter. Field records, corroborated by data from captive-reared individuals that were subsequently released, indicate that the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days], a full year of life dedicated to exploration, host-species recognition, and territory establishment before any reproductive effort begins.

This extended lifespan is notable for a bird of such modest body mass and may be a life-history consequence of the low extrinsic mortality rates associated with a brood-parasitic strategy, which reduces the time adults spend vulnerable to predators at a nest site. The egg itself shows distinctive dimensions that facilitate successful parasitism. Precise measurements of a representative sample of eggs yield a mean length of 1.99 centimeters and a mean width of 1.47 centimeters; estimating the mass from these linear dimensions using the standard formula for an ellipsoid yields a calculated fresh egg mass of approximately 2.25 grams, a value that aligns well with the known energetic investment per offspring for a bird of this size. The close correspondence between the calculated value from the egg dimensions and the direct hatchling mass suggests efficient yolk-to-tissue conversion during the 11-day incubation period (approximately 11 days) [ab = approximately 11 days] at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], with minimal loss of energy to metabolic heat production.

Habitat preferences of the Pavonine cuckoo are strongly tied to undisturbed lowland forest and mature secondary growth, where the density of potential avian hosts reaches its peak. Within these habitats, the species exploits a wide array of passerine foster parents, though a preference for furnariid and tyrannid nests has been noted across multiple study sites. The single-egg parasitism strategy, combined with a maximum reproductive rate of approximately nine eggs per year [Ri = approximately nine eggs per year], each laid in a distinct host nest [N_R_i = each laid in a distinct host nest], imposes a strong selective premium on the female's ability to locate and monitor an adequate number of active host nests throughout the breeding season. Behavioral observations indicate that individual females maintain cognitive maps of dozens of potential host territories and time their visits with remarkable precision. The species' vocal repertoire, including a distinctive descending whistle, is thought to function both in intraspecific communication between widely dispersed individuals and in the assessment of host nest activity. Future research focusing on the genetic structuring of host-specific races would greatly illuminate the microevolutionary processes driving the diversification of this and related neotropical cuckoo species.
